THOUGHT: Young adult with sudden sharp low back pain during exercise that radiates down the leg into the foot — a classic radicular distribution suggesting sciatica. Positive straight leg raise test supports nerve root tension. MRI confirms an L5–S1 disc herniation impinging an adjacent nerve root, providing an anatomic cause; L5–S1 herniation typically affects the S1 root with pain down the posterior/lateral leg to the foot. Neurologic exam is largely intact (no significant weakness or reflex loss, and sensation preserved), which can occur with partial or early compression. Absence of fever, weight loss, or bowel/bladder changes and normal vitals make infection, malignancy, and cauda equina syndrome unlikely. Putting these together, the most likely diagnosis is acute lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica) from an L5–S1 herniated disc compressing the S1 nerve root.

DIAGNOSIS: Acute lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica) due to L5–S1 herniated nucleus pulposus compressing the S1 nerve root.
